newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Late selling breaks Australian dlr range monotony.
newsitem.headline: Late selling breaks Australian dlr range monotony.

text.p: Late selling pressure took the Australian dollar to its lows for the day, after an otherwise quiet day which saw most of the market attention focused on U.S. dollar/yen trading.

While the selling broke the monotony of the 20 point range in which the local unit had spent most of the day, it did not amount to a serious threat on the unit's broader US$0.7800/7900 range seen since mid-March, traders said.
By 4.30 p.m. (0630 GMT), the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7840/45, down on an opening US$0.7855/60 and a local close on Tuesday of US$0.7872/77.
Traders said the unit would find good buying interest on any dips, just as it would run into willing sellers, said to be options-related, on moves towards US$0.7900.

"Down at the low 78 (cents), the US$0.7815/25 area, there's still some good domestic buying. But there's a lot of option related sellling, I'm told, up around that US$0.7890/7900 level as well, so it's pretty well trapped up at the moment," one trader said.
"I can't see that we're going to get out of it in a hurry, unless we see a big swing in the (U.S.) dollar," he said.
At the lows there was a mix of domestic and offshore buying, including some through the afternoon that appeared to have been related to an upcoming samurai issue, traders said.

However, the offshore volumes were not sufficient to give the impetus for a major move and traders said given the uncertainty over U.S. interest rates, stock market and trade tensions with Japan, locals would be happy to be sidelined.

"There doesn't seem a lot of big fresh flows coming through from offshore at the moment -- a lot of bits and pieces, but nothing of any volume, so the locals are quite content just to hang in there for the moment," the trader said.
The main focus on the day was on U.S. dollar/yen, after comments by U.S Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin overnight sent the dollar down to a low of 121.40 yen.
Rubin, who will visit Japan on Friday, said that he would not welcome a reversal in the progress Japan has made in cutting its trade surplus.
However, some of the dollar's losses were recouped when the Bank of Japan's tankan survey of business sentiment for March came in line with expectations.

The survey showed improved confidence amongst large manufacturers but ongoing weakness in non-manufacturers and smaller firms, and alleviated concerns that Japan rates may have had a higher bias after the report.

"In the near term, the minimal chance of a Japanese rate hike should underpin the Australian dollar/yen, as interest rate differentials continue to favour the Australian dollar," Westpac economists said in a commentary.
The Australian dollar ended at 96.15/25 yen, up on an early 95.75/85, but well down on Tuesday's closing 97.26/36. In trade weighted terms, it ended at 60.3 from a previous close of 60.5.
Traders said offshore events would continue to provide the main influences on the local market on Thursday.
Thursday's balance of trade on goods and services is not expected to cause too much commotion in the markets, with traders placing more emphasis on Friday's retail trade figures.
The trade data is expected to show a deficit of around A$13 million, down on January's A$63 million shortfall. Forecasts range from a A$200 million surplus to a A$250 million deficit.
